lesson.title: Beyond Heat: Introducing Enthalpy
lesson.summary: Enthalpy, symbolized H, is a thermodynamic quantity defined so that at constant pressure, the most common condition for real chemical reactions, the heat exchanged with the surroundings equals the change in enthalpy exactly.
lesson.body:
In your study of thermodynamics you met internal energy, U, and the first law, delta U = q + w, which tracks both heat exchanged and work done as a system changes. That bookkeeping is complete, but it is inconvenient for chemistry, because most reactions happen in open beakers or flasks, exposed to the atmosphere, where gases can expand or contract against constant atmospheric pressure. Every one of those reactions does a small amount of pressure volume work on or against the surroundings, and tracking that work term separately every single time would be tedious. Chemists solved this by defining a new quantity, enthalpy, H = U + PV, that folds pressure volume work directly into a single state function.

The payoff of this definition shows up the moment pressure is held constant, which is exactly the situation for a reaction open to the atmosphere. At constant pressure, it can be shown that delta H = delta U + P delta V, and this combination is exactly equal to the heat exchanged at constant pressure, q(p). In short, delta H = q(p). This is the direct link back to heat transfer: enthalpy change is simply the name given to heat flow whenever a process happens at constant pressure, which describes the overwhelming majority of chemistry done in an open container, from a beaker on a bench to a reaction happening in the open air.

Like internal energy, enthalpy is a state function, meaning its value depends only on the current state of a system, not on the path taken to get there, and it is an extensive property, scaling with the amount of material present. The sign of delta H tells you the direction heat flows: a negative delta H means the system releases heat to its surroundings, an exothermic process, while a positive delta H means the system absorbs heat from its surroundings, an endothermic process.

As an example, consider 5.00 g of solid NaOH dissolved in 100.0 g of water inside an open, coffee cup style container, so the process happens at constant atmospheric pressure. The initial temperature is 22.0 degrees C and the final temperature, after the NaOH fully dissolves, is 33.7 degrees C. Treating the total solution mass as 105.0 g (100.0 g water plus 5.00 g NaOH) with a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g times degree C), the heat absorbed by the solution is q = m c delta T = (105.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(33.7 minus 22.0) = (438.9 J/degree C)(11.7 degrees C) = 5,135.1 J, or 5.14 kJ. Since this heat was absorbed by the solution, it must have been released by the dissolving process, so q(process) = negative 5.14 kJ, and because the container was open to the atmosphere, delta H = q(p) = negative 5.14 kJ for this 5.00 g sample. Converting to a molar basis using the molar mass of NaOH, 40.00 g/mol, gives 5.00 g divided by 40.00 g/mol = 0.1250 mol, so delta H = negative 5.14 kJ divided by 0.1250 mol = negative 41.1 kJ/mol, confirming that dissolving NaOH in water is an exothermic process, consistent with the temperature rise observed.
